content: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a genetic disorder that primarily affects the respiratory and digestive systems. It impacts approximately 35,000 individuals in the United States. The condition is characterized by the production of abnormally thick and sticky mucus, which can obstruct airways, leading to lung damage, and trap bacteria, increasing the risk of infections. Additionally, this thick mucus prevents digestive enzymes from reaching the intestines, impairing the body’s ability to absorb nutrients from food. CF can affect multiple organs, making individuals more susceptible to complications such as diabetes, liver disease (cirrhosis), arthritis, acid reflux, hypersplenism (an overactive spleen), and osteoporosis. The symptoms of CF can vary but often include salty-tasting skin, a persistent cough that may produce thick mucus or blood, wheezing or shortness of breath, frequent lung or sinus infections, nasal polyps (growths in the nasal passages), poor growth or weight gain during childhood, greasy and foul-smelling stools, constipation, and male infertility. If you or your child exhibit any of these symptoms, it is important to consult a healthcare provider. Diagnostic tests, such as a sweat test or genetic testing, may be necessary to confirm the presence of CF. If a diagnosis is made, specialized care can be sought at a Cystic Fibrosis Care Center. CF is caused by mutations in the Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator (CFTR) gene, which provides instructions for producing the CFTR protein. This protein plays a critical role in regulating the movement of salt and water in and out of cells. Every individual inherits two copies of the CFTR gene, one from each parent. For a person to develop CF, they must inherit mutations in both copies of the CFTR gene. Parents who each carry a mutation in one copy of the CFTR gene, but do not have CF themselves, can pass the condition to their child if the child inherits the mutated gene from both parents. Carrier screening for CF is recommended for individuals who are pregnant or planning a pregnancy. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists advises that this screening be offered to all prospective parents. However, it is important to note that carrier screening does not test for all possible CFTR mutations. If you have a family history of CF, it is essential to inform your healthcare provider so that testing can be tailored to detect the specific mutation present in your family. Genetic counseling may also be recommended in such cases. In the United States, all newborns are screened for CF shortly after birth as part of routine newborn screening programs. Early detection is crucial, as it allows for the initiation of treatment to delay or prevent complications associated with the disorder. While some individuals with CF may exhibit symptoms shortly after birth, others, particularly those with milder forms of the condition, may not show signs until later in life. Treatment for CF has advanced significantly, enabling individuals with the condition to live longer and healthier lives. The primary goals of treatment are to improve respiratory and digestive function, prevent and manage infections, and reduce mucus buildup. Treatment options include medications, therapies to clear mucus from the lungs, and, in severe cases, lung transplantation. Recent pharmacogenomic advancements have led to the development of targeted therapies that address the underlying cause of CF. These medications are designed to correct the specific effects of certain CFTR mutations, but their use is limited to individuals with those particular genetic changes.
